taxonomy.subtopic: Venous outflow obstruction and hemorrhagic infarction

questions.stem_html:
A 15-year-old boy awakens with sudden severe left scrotal pain and vomiting. The left testis is high-riding and horizontally oriented, and the cremasteric reflex is absent. Doppler ultrasonography shows markedly reduced intratesticular flow. Emergency exploration confirms twisting of the spermatic cord.

Which pathologic sequence occurs first after torsion?

options.text_html: Arterial rupture causes immediate pale coagulative necrosis without congestion
Autoimmune orchitis develops before vascular compromise
Bacterial ascent through the vas deferens causes suppurative infarction
Thin-walled venous and lymphatic channels collapse before arterial inflow, causing congestion and hemorrhagic infarction
Seminiferous tubules obstruct the pampiniform plexus through intraluminal casts

questions.explanation_html: Twisting compresses the low-pressure venous and lymphatic outflow first. Continued arterial inflow into an obstructed bed causes swelling and hemorrhage, followed by arterial compromise and infarction. Venous obstruction explains the early congestion, edema, and hemorrhagic character of torsion injury.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Torsion first impairs venous outflow, so congestion and hemorrhage precede complete arterial failure.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Autoimmune inflammation is not the initiating event in acute torsion.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Ascending infection causes epididymo-orchitis and usually preserves the cremasteric reflex.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: The vascular pedicle twists externally; seminiferous tubular casts are not the cause.

questions.educational_objective: Recognize testicular torsion as a vascular emergency in which venous outflow is lost before arterial inflow, producing hemorrhagic infarction.
